Kyriakos Axiotis, Staff Research Scientist, and Thomas Fu, Principal Engineer, Google Research

We present DeepCrossAttention (DCA), an architecture that enhances transformer networks by using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention to dynamically combine outputs from previous layers, preventing the information dilution seen in traditional residual connections. Presented in our ICML 2025 paper, this architectural improvement allows models to achieve the same quality up to three times faster with a negligible increase in parameters.

Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.

To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections, also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.

The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.

In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.

Instead of treating skip connections as a rigid, additive pipeline, DCA reframes residual learning as a dynamic routing problem. Rather than passing all prior layers forward with equal weight, DCA introduces a lightweight, layer-wise module that decides how to best combine previous embeddings on a per-token basis.

Comparison between a standard residual network and DeepCrossAttention (DCA). While a standard residual network uses rigid, additive point-wise connections with equal weighting, DCA introduces dynamic, learned routing weights (W) that allow each layer to selectively route and combine features from across the history of preceding layers.

By allowing the network to dynamically select and retrieve high-resolution features from earlier layers, DCA eliminates the information dilution inherent to classic residual connections.

To test whether DCA can overcome information dilution in practice, we evaluated our approach across controlled synthetic setups, large-scale language modeling benchmarks, and image classification tasks.

DCA demonstrated significant improvements in convergence speed, training stability, and final model quality across these experiments.

original_summary: Open a pull request and get back to building. Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team's policy allows.
article_content:
Anyone who has opened a pull request knows how this goes. They start on the next thing, and then the review comes back. So they stop, dig back into the old code, push a fix, and wait for the review to run again. Then they go find someone to approve it.

There's a good reason it works this way. Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.

That's why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta. It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what's ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.

Claude Ship is made up of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don't have to manage each step manually.

Code Review performs an in-depth review of pull requests against the codebase through multiple lenses. It collects findings, adversarially verifies them, categorizes them, and posts them to a PR. On the Claude Code team, where Claude's review is one layer of a broader process, merged PRs more than doubled from June to September while the share reverted fell by more than 40%. Code Review gives teams fast reviews, clear findings, and a choice of Quick, Standard, or Deep review levels for each repository.

PR Steward works to keep a PR green, but is designed not to approve or merge pull requests. It jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members. After every push, it comments with what it changed and how to undo it. Developers can comment @claude with an instruction to steer the work, or @claude stop to have it step back.

From there, Claude Approvals applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios. It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file. Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language. For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light.

Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code. When a change is ready, they run /ship. Claude pushes it, opens the PR, reviews the change, and works on feedback and failing checks to help get it ready to merge. What can merge depends on the developer's permissions and the repository's branch rules.

Turning Claude Ship on for an entire repository puts it to work across a team's pull requests automatically, under settings and an approval policy the team controls. Developers don't need to manually invoke the /ship command.

Teams set the pace. They can start with one repository, choose a review level and when reviews run, set a monthly spend limit, and run their approval policy in observe mode until they trust it.

We run Claude Ship on many of our own pull requests. One of the biggest changes is who can act on customer feedback. For example, a product manager on the Claude Code team can now read a piece of feedback, talk through ideas and tradeoffs with Claude Tag, have it open a PR, and move on to the next thing while Claude Ship takes it through review, fixes, and an approval decision.
